annotations.title: Vitamin B12 - Health Professional Fact Sheet

content.text:
For most people, **there isn’t a defined “too much” amount of vitamin B12**: the NIH says **no tolerable upper intake level (UL) has been established** because B12 has **low toxicity**, even at high doses. ([ods.od.nih.gov](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminB12-HealthProfessional/?uid=c273e26eea9a1s16&utm_source=openai))

That said:

- **Recommended daily amount for adults:** about **2.4 mcg/day**.
- Common supplements are often **500–1,000 mcg/day**, which is far above the daily requirement but usually considered safe because only a small amount is absorbed and excess is excreted.
- **Very high doses** are usually only needed for **documented deficiency**, malabsorption, vegan diets, pernicious anemia, certain meds like metformin or acid blockers, or after bariatric surgery.

**When it may be “too much” in practice:**  
If you’re taking high-dose B12 without a reason, have **high blood B12 on labs**, or develop side effects like **acne/rosacea flare, diarrhea, headache, nausea, or palpitations**, it’s worth stopping or lowering the dose and asking a clinician. Mayo Clinic notes high doses can cause side effects in some people. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-vitamin-b12/art-20363663?p=1&utm_source=openai))

A simple rule of thumb: **If you’re not deficient, 1,000+ mcg daily is usually unnecessary**, even if it’s generally safe. A standard multivitamin or occasional lower-dose B12 is usually enough unless your doctor recommended more.
